client: Lately, I’ve been feeling so overwhelmed with sadness since my grandmother passed away last month. It’s been hard to process my own grief, and I feel like I don’t know how to support my mom—she’s struggling so much, and I just don’t know what to say or do. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with something like this—it feels like it’s just something we have to get through on our own.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of pain right now, both for yourself and for your mom. Grief can feel so heavy, especially when you’re trying to navigate it while also supporting someone else. What thoughts come up for you when you say it feels like something you have to get through on your own?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I feel like grief is just something personal and private—like no one else can really understand what I’m going through, even a therapist. And I don’t want to burden anyone with it, especially my mom. She’s already dealing with so much, and I don’t want to add to her pain by talking about mine. It feels like I should just keep it to myself and push through.
therapist: It sounds like you’re holding onto a lot of your own grief to protect your mom, which must feel like a heavy responsibility. Grief can feel isolating, but it’s also something that many people experience in their own way—does it feel like sharing your feelings might help, even if it’s with someone outside your family?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess sharing might help, but it’s hard to imagine opening up to someone else. I feel like they’ll just tell me things like “time heals all wounds” or “she’s in a better place,” and that doesn’t really help me. It feels like people don’t know what to say, and I end up feeling even more alone. I’m not sure how talking about it here would be any different.
therapist: It sounds like you’ve had experiences where others’ responses didn’t feel helpful or comforting, and that’s left you feeling even more disconnected. I wonder if part of what’s hard is feeling like people don’t truly understand what you’re going through—would it feel different here if we focused less on “fixing” it and more on simply being with those feelings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually sounds kind of comforting—just being with the feelings instead of trying to fix them. I think I’ve been putting so much pressure on myself to “handle” this grief perfectly, and it’s exhausting. But I’m still not sure how to let myself just feel it without feeling overwhelmed or like I’m failing somehow. It’s hard to trust that it’s okay to be messy right now.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to notice the pressure you’ve been putting on yourself to grieve in a certain way, and that’s a big step. Grief is rarely neat or tidy—what would it feel like to give yourself permission to be messy, even if just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels really scary to let myself be messy—like if I let myself feel everything, I might just fall apart and not be able to pull myself back together. And I don’t want to burden anyone with that, especially my mom. But I guess it’s also exhausting to keep pretending I’m okay when I’m not. I’m just not sure how to balance those two things.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying this fear of falling apart alongside the exhaustion of holding it all together—that must feel like such a difficult tension to hold. What comes up for you when you imagine someone—maybe even yourself—offering you the same compassion you’re trying to give your mom?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea kind of makes me uncomfortable, to be honest. I don't really know how to accept compassion for myself - it feels selfish when my mom is hurting so much more than I am. And part of me wonders if I even deserve that kindness when I haven't been strong enough for her. It's easier to focus on her pain than to look at my own.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of guilt tied up in the idea of giving yourself compassion—like it might take something away from your mom or mean you’re not being strong enough for her. What would it feel like to consider that caring for yourself might actually help you be more present for her, rather than taking away from her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a really hard idea for me to sit with. Part of me knows you're probably right, but another part feels like if I stop beating myself up, I'll somehow stop caring as much about my mom's pain. It's like this guilt is the only thing keeping me connected to her grief right now.
therapist: It sounds like you’re holding onto guilt as a way to stay connected to your mom’s grief, and that makes a lot of sense—it’s like it’s become a protective bridge between you and her pain. I wonder, though, if there might be other ways to stay connected to her without carrying the weight of guilt? What might that look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I’ve never really thought about guilt being a bridge before—that feels true in a way. But I don’t know how else to stay connected to her. What if I stop feeling guilty and she thinks I don’t care anymore? It’s scary to imagine letting go of that, even if it’s heavy. I don’t know what a different kind of connection would look like.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has felt like a lifeline to your mom, and the idea of letting it go brings up real fear—like you might lose that connection entirely. I hear how deeply you care about her, even in your worry. What would it feel like to explore other ways of being there for her—maybe ways that don’t ask you to carry so much pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don’t know… maybe sharing small memories of grandma together instead of just sitting in silence? But it still feels selfish to make it about me in any way. What if she thinks I’m trying to move on too fast? I don’t want her to feel like I’m abandoning my grief—or hers.
therapist: It sounds like sharing memories feels like it could be a meaningful way to connect, but there’s also a lot of worry about how it might come across—like it could be seen as moving on too quickly or making it about you. What comes up for you when you think about approaching it as something you could do *with* her, rather than *for* her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess doing it *with* her feels a little less scary than trying to fix things *for* her. But I still worry she'll see it as me trying to rush her healing process. What if my way of grieving—wanting to talk about memories—feels wrong to her? I don't want to make things worse by trying to connect in the wrong way.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding back from sharing memories not because you don't care, but because you're so deeply attuned to your mom's needs—that's actually very loving. What if you started small—maybe just sharing one memory and then checking in with her about how it felt for her? That way you're not assuming what she needs, but creating space to discover it together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
